title: Continuity
summary: A function is continuous at $a$ when $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a)$ — no holes, jumps, or blowups. Continuity on an interval lets you substitute to find limits and guarantees the Intermediate Value Theorem, which locates roots.

continuity at a point.plain: No break at $a$: the graph connects through $(a,f(a))$.
continuity at a point.in_class: Requires $f(a)$ defined, $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ exists, and the two are equal.

removable discontinuity.plain: A single missing point — a hole you could 'plug'.
removable discontinuity.in_class: The limit exists but $f(a)$ is missing or wrong; redefining $f(a)$ fixes it.

jump discontinuity.plain: The graph leaps from one value to another.
jump discontinuity.in_class: Left and right limits exist but disagree; common in piecewise functions.

infinite discontinuity.plain: The function shoots to $\pm\infty$ at the point.
infinite discontinuity.in_class: Occurs at vertical asymptotes, e.g. $1/x$ at $x=0$.

continuous on an interval.plain: No breaks anywhere across a stretch of $x$-values.
continuous on an interval.in_class: Polynomials are continuous everywhere; rationals except where the denominator is zero.

Intermediate Value Theorem.plain: A continuous function hits every value between its endpoints.
Intermediate Value Theorem.in_class: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and $N$ lies between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, some $c$ gives $f(c)=N$ — proves roots exist.

one-sided continuity.plain: Continuous approaching from just one side.
one-sided continuity.in_class: Needed at the endpoints of a closed interval.

piecewise function.plain: A function defined by different rules on different intervals.
piecewise function.in_class: Check continuity where the rules meet.

concept_sections.heading: The three-part test
concept_sections.explanation: $f$ is continuous at $a$ exactly when three things hold: $f(a)$ is defined, $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ exists, and they are equal. If any part fails, there is a discontinuity there.
math_steps: Check the two are equal; all three ⇒ continuous.

concept_sections.heading: Types of discontinuity
concept_sections.explanation: Discontinuities come in three flavors: removable (a hole where the limit exists but the value is missing/wrong), jump (left and right limits differ), and infinite (the function blows up to $\pm\infty$).
math_steps: Removable: limit exists, value doesn't match — a plug-able hole.

concept_sections.heading: Continuity on intervals
concept_sections.explanation: Polynomials are continuous for all $x$. Rational, root, trig, exponential, and log functions are continuous everywhere they are defined. Sums, products, quotients, and compositions of continuous functions stay continuous.
math_steps: Exclude points where it's undefined (division by zero, negative under an even root).

concept_sections.heading: Making a piecewise function continuous
concept_sections.explanation: At a boundary between pieces, continuity requires the two pieces to meet: the left value equals the right value. Choose the unknown constant so the one-sided limits agree with the function value.
math_steps: Compute the left-hand limit at the boundary.
Set them equal (and equal to $f$ there) and solve for the constant.

concept_sections.heading: The Intermediate Value Theorem
concept_sections.explanation: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and a target value $N$ lies between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, then $f(c)=N$ for some $c$ in between. In particular, a sign change guarantees a root.

real_world_examples.title: A thermostat's temperature record
real_world_examples.scenario: Room temperature changes smoothly over the day.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Temperature is a continuous function of time, so between a morning low and afternoon high it must pass through every value in between — the Intermediate Value Theorem.

real_world_examples.title: A jump in a parking fee
real_world_examples.scenario: A garage charges a flat rate that jumps at each hour.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The cost is a step (piecewise) function with jump discontinuities exactly at each hour mark.

real_world_examples.title: Finding a root by bisection
real_world_examples.scenario: A calculator hunts for where an equation equals zero.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Because the function is continuous and changes sign, the IVT guarantees a root, and bisection zeroes in on it.

problems.prompt: What kind of discontinuity does $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-1}{x-1}$ have at $x=1$?
solution_steps: The limit is $2$ but $f(1)$ is undefined.
problems.hint: Limit exists but the point is missing.

problems.prompt: Find $k$ so that $f(x)=\begin{cases}x+3,&x\le1\\ kx,&x>1\end{cases}$ is continuous.

solution_steps: The limit is $4$ but the value doesn't exist.
problems.hint: Undefined value ⇒ not continuous, even if the limit exists.
Even roots need a nonnegative inside.

solution_steps: By the IVT a root lies in $(0,1)$.
problems.hint: Look for a sign change and cite the IVT.

problems.prompt: Find $a,b$ so $f(x)=\begin{cases}x^2,&x\le1\\ ax+b,&x>1\end{cases}$ is continuous with $f(2)=5$.
The function $f(x)=\lfloor x\rfloor$ (floor) is discontinuous at which $x$?
solution_steps: Floor jumps by 1 at each whole number.
Left and right limits differ there.
problems.hint: Think about where the step function leaps.
